solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Highlight hair after sex

indicators.note: after says the piece meaning hair is placed second, behind the piece meaning sex

parts.note: S is a standard abbreviation for sex, as on forms
a tress is a long lock of hair

explanation.surface: A hairdresser's appointment booked for after a romantic encounter, with some highlights put in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Highlight' looks like a hairdressing term alongside 'hair', but it is the verb meaning emphasise; 'after' puts the hair piece behind the sex piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To highlight a point is to put emphasis on it, which is exactly what laying stress on it means.

clue.text: Bully's balls hoisted — mad cheer all round!

indicators.note: in a down entry, hoisting something lifts it so it reads from bottom to top
all round says the jumbled letters surround the other piece completely
something mad is deranged, so the following word's letters are put out of order

parts.note: taken as written, to be jumbled
balls is slang for nonsense, which is rot

explanation.surface: A bully's testicles are yanked upward while a crazed crowd cheers around him.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled cheer splits as HEC...ER around the reversed TOR; the 's stands for 'is', joining definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A hectorer is someone who browbeats or intimidates others with loud domineering talk, the behaviour of a bully.

clue.text: Where to get rid of your pounds at an incredible rate?

definitions.text: Where to get rid of your pounds at an incredible rate?

parts.words: Where to get rid of your pounds at an incredible rate?
parts.note: surface reading: a place where money is spent extravagantly fast

parts.words: Where to get rid of your pounds at an incredible rate?
parts.note: setter's reading: pounds are units of body weight, shed rapidly at a residential slimming resort

explanation.walkthrough: Pounds can be money or weight; the clue also hints that such resorts are pricey, so both senses apply.
explanation.definitionFit: A fat farm is an informal name for a residential health spa where clients go on diets and exercise programmes to slim down.

clue.text: All show, Gordon-like?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: showy and ostentatious, style over substance
second meaning: resembling Flash Gordon, the comic-strip space hero, so 'like Flash'

explanation.walkthrough: In Private Eye 'Gordon' suggests Gordon Brown, the far from flashy prime minister; the question mark flags the comic hero Flash Gordon instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Something flashy is gaudy and ostentatious, all surface display; playfully, it also means taking after Flash Gordon.

clue.text: Has-been PM broken, à la Brown?

indicators.note: broken things fall to pieces, so the following letters are reassembled in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, accent dropped, to be jumbled

explanation.surface: A former prime minister left a broken man, just as Gordon Brown was.
explanation.walkthrough: Andrew Bonar Law was briefly prime minister in 1922-23 and is now largely forgotten, hence 'has-been'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonar Law led a Conservative government in the early 1920s, so he is a past premier of Britain.

clue.text: Wacky as a Cold War souvenir?

definitions.note: a phrase describing a souvenir, not the noun itself
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a chunk literally taken from the Berlin Wall, a popular keepsake after 1989

explanation.surface: Is a Cold War keepsake a bit of a crackpot item?
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means bizarre or unconventional; literally, Berlin Wall fragments were chipped off that barrier and sold as mementos.

clue.text: Dead-beat OK for hanging?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: suitable (fit) for the gallows drop, read literally

explanation.walkthrough: Dead-beat is the British sense of worn out, not a layabout; the question mark warns the second sense is literal gallows humour.
explanation.definitionFit: Being ready to collapse with tiredness is the idiom; literally, a condemned person passed as fit for the trapdoor.

clue.text: Sex serial broadcast

definitions.meaning: first meaning: getting one's ... is British slang for having sex

definitions.note: a cryptic hint: the spoken word serial matches a breakfast grain
definitions.meaning: second meaning: serial spoken aloud is cereal, and these grains are a cereal

explanation.surface: A racy drama serial on television.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting your oats is a British idiom for sexual activity, and the grain is a cereal crop eaten as porridge.

clue.text: see 24dn.
(&11ac.) Our press revelations the reprehensible way

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Private Eye's long-running column exposing Fleet Street journalism
second meaning: way is a street and reprehensible is shameful, read word by word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Our' is Private Eye speaking: Street of Shame is its nickname for Fleet Street, historic home of the London newspapers, and the title of its media gossip page.
explanation.definitionFit: The magazine's column on tabloid misdeeds bears this title, and literally it is a road deserving disgrace.

clue.text: see 10ac.
Despised organ player's shy speech hesitancy

parts.note: to shy something is to throw or fling it
er is the sound of hesitating while speaking

explanation.surface: A disliked church organist who stammers shyly when talking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shy' looks like an adjective about the organist but is the verb throw. Tosser is a crude British insult, literally a masturbator, hence the 'organ player'.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang this is a vulgar term of contempt for an obnoxious man, literally one who handles his own member.

clue.text: In which Brenda might overlook the action of one of her lot needing genital protection

definitions.text: In which Brenda might overlook the action

parts.note: a member of the Queen's family is a royal
a box is the protective cup a cricketer wears over the groin

explanation.surface: The Queen watches a match while one of her relatives needs a groin guard.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for Queen Elizabeth II.
explanation.definitionFit: The reserved enclosure for the monarch at a theatre or sports ground gives her a view over the performance or play.

clue.text: Received wisdom of unashamed "Toryhood": get vote in!

indicators.note: get with in instructs that one piece be put inside the other
unashamed suggests letting it all hang out without restraint, so the quoted word is set loose and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be jumbled
voters mark a cross, X, on the ballot paper

explanation.surface: Brazen Conservative values have become conventional wisdom: go and vote for them!
explanation.walkthrough: The cross goes in near the end of the jumbled letters, before the final Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Orthodoxy is the generally accepted set of beliefs, the views everyone has been taught to hold.

clue.text: Bieber composition 'Right for Ecstasy' — unknown way to get co-operation from the Met?

definitions.text: way to get co-operation from the Met?

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, so the letters are arranged afresh
one thing for another means swapping it in place of the other

parts.note: the pop singer's name, taken as written
R is the usual abbreviation for right
E is slang for the drug ecstasy
in algebra y is an unknown quantity

explanation.surface: A Justin Bieber song title, then a jibe about how to get the police on your side.
explanation.walkthrough: One E in the singer's name becomes R, the result is jumbled, and Y follows. The Met is London's Metropolitan Police, whose officers were embroiled in a payments-for-stories scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: Paying off officers is a corrupt method of securing their help; the question mark marks the satirical swipe at the police.

clue.text: Clinton to pack up? There could well be money in it

definitions.text: There could well be money in it

parts.note: Bill Clinton, the former US president
to fold is to give up or close down, as a business does

explanation.surface: Is Bill Clinton about to quit? His lucrative speaking career suggests otherwise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'There could well be money in it' sounds like a comment on Clinton's earnings, but it simply describes a wallet.
explanation.definitionFit: A billfold is the American word for a wallet, a folding case for carrying banknotes.

clue.text: Fools one thousand at Women's Institute beset by booze problem

indicators.note: beset by means surrounded on all sides, so the trouble wraps around the other letters

parts.note: the DTs, delirium tremens, are the shakes suffered by heavy drinkers
I is the Roman numeral for one
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
WI is the abbreviation for the Women's Institute, a British countrywomen's organisation

explanation.surface: A thousand idiots at a Women's Institute meeting, plagued by a drink problem.
explanation.definitionFit: Dimwits are stupid people, and to call someone a fool is to call them the same thing.

clue.text: Sums up England team's ambitions, right? Hissed, end of Brazilian fiasco

definitions.note: the definition is a phrase describing a state; the answer completes 'the ambitions are ...'

indicators.note: a fiasco is a total mess, so the letters land in disorder

parts.note: R is the usual abbreviation for right
taken as written

indicators.note: end of picks out only the final letter of the following word

parts.note: the final letter of Brazilian

explanation.surface: England's football World Cup hopes, jeered off in a Brazilian disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls England's dismal 2014 World Cup in Brazil.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopes that are in shreds are torn apart and ruined, which describes the team's dashed tournament ambitions.

clue.text: Who'll save us all from Amis (he's "diversifying")?

indicators.note: diversifying means branching out into varied forms, so the letters take a different shape

parts.note: the novelist Martin Amis's name, taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A dig at novelist Martin Amis branching out, as though he thinks himself our saviour.
explanation.definitionFit: A messiah is a promised deliverer or saviour, the figure expected to rescue everyone.

clue.text: Multinational, sanctimonious and ultimately insatiable, which sums up good old American values

definitions.text: which sums up good old American values
definitions.note: a relative clause describing the answer rather than a noun synonym

parts.note: Apple is a giant multinational technology company
pi is crossword shorthand for pious, self-righteous

indicators.note: ultimately points to what comes last, so only the final letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the final letter of insatiable

explanation.surface: A jab at a greedy, self-righteous corporation embodying American values.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying 'as American as apple pie' makes the dessert a byword for wholesome traditional American life.

clue.text: Mount and shag on getting high

parts.note: to pull is British slang for picking up a sexual partner
up means high, raised aloft

explanation.surface: A crude description of sex while intoxicated.
explanation.walkthrough: Shag is British slang for having sex.
explanation.definitionFit: A pull-up is a mount on which someone hauls themselves upward, as on a raised bar or a climb.

clue.text: see 24dn.
Heath's last vent against party, shock style

indicators.note: last means only the final letter of the possessive word is taken

parts.note: the final letter of Heath, the 's being possessive
to vent an opinion is to air it
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: Former PM Edward Heath venting his final grievance against his own party.
explanation.walkthrough: Shock is a mass of hair, as in a shock of hair, so 'shock style' is a hairstyle.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairdo is the arrangement of one's hair, and a shock is a thick mop of it.

clue.text: Refuse, being disenchanted with Clinton's vice

parts.note: to be off something is to have lost one's enthusiasm for it
Al Gore was Bill Clinton's vice-president

explanation.surface: Someone turns down an offer, having lost faith in Clinton's moral failing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vice' suggests the president's sexual misconduct, but it means his vice-president.
explanation.definitionFit: Offal is the entrails and organs of a slaughtered animal, and also discarded waste or rubbish.

clue.text: (&22ac.+ 9dn.)Habit that Cameron and chums have in common, so too chilled out?

definitions.text: Habit that Cameron and chums have in common

indicators.note: out here means disordered, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be jumbled

explanation.surface: The relaxed manner shared by David Cameron and his Etonian friends.
explanation.walkthrough: Habit means clothing as well as custom: Cameron and his cabinet chums shared the Eton tie and the loyalty it stands for.
explanation.definitionFit: The neckwear of a public school stands for the network of privilege binding its former pupils together.

clue.text: Virus spread by very old Russian leader who goes on and on

indicators.note: spread means scattered about, so the letters are dispersed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be jumbled
V is the usual abbreviation for very
O is the usual abbreviation for old

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the initial letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of Russian

explanation.surface: An infection passed on by an ageing Russian ruler who clings to power indefinitely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Russian leader who goes on and on' suggests a long-serving Kremlin figure, but the leader is just R.
explanation.definitionFit: A survivor is someone who endures and keeps going despite hardships that defeat others.

clue.text: Big star ego round Clegg's no.2

parts.note: the id and ego are paired parts of the psyche in Freud; id stands for the self here
O is round in shape

indicators.note: number two picks out the second letter of the possessive name

parts.note: the second letter of Clegg

explanation.surface: A self-important celebrity orbiting Nick Clegg, his deputy.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick Clegg was literally the number two, Deputy Prime Minister, in the 2010 coalition.
explanation.definitionFit: An idol is a celebrity worshipped by fans, a superstar adored by the public.

clue.text: No subsidy for us, being without a monocle?

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase hinting at the answer as a state of vision

parts.note: given no financial aid, so unaided
'us' is Private Eye speaking of itself

explanation.surface: Private Eye complains about getting no subsidy, its monocled mascot Lord Gnome going without.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye's cover mascot, Lord Gnome, sports a monocle, which the definition plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: Seeing without a lens or optical device means looking with nothing but natural sight.
